841.title: Mystery plays
841.hook: townspeople acted the Bible on wagons: the shipwrights built Noah's ark
841.howItsDone: Some English towns, including York and Chester, still stage their mystery plays, sometimes on wagons in the streets, and some churches put on nativity plays with children at Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nubia's churches: painted faces found under the sand by the Nile. Your line was remembered churches.

A summer morning in an English town, and a wooden wagon creaks around the corner. On it, a man with a hammer is building a boat. He's playing Noah, and the men helping him build real boats all week: they're the town's shipwrights. The wagon moves on to the next corner, and another rolls up behind it with the next story. On one of them, later, the crowd laughs when Noah's wife refuses to get on board. All day long, the whole Bible comes down the street.

Mystery plays were cycles of short Bible plays, put on by ordinary townspeople in English towns like York and Chester. They usually ran from creation to the last judgment: the fall, Noah, Abraham and Isaac, the shepherds at Bethlehem, the crucifixion, the empty tomb. Each play was given to a trade guild, and the guilds often got the scene that fit their work. In York, the shipwrights staged the building of the ark. In Genesis, God tells Noah, in the King James Bible, "Make thee an ark of gopher wood." And then, "Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he." Who better to swing those hammers? Each play went up on a pageant wagon, a stage on wheels, and the wagons stopped at set places so different crowds could see each scene in turn. The plays were in English, the language people spoke at home, at a time when church services were in Latin. They mixed holy and ordinary. Shepherds grumble about the cold before the angel comes. Noah's wife, in some plays, would rather stay with her friends than climb into the ark. People laughed, and then they watched a carpenter's son die on a cross. A town that acted these stories year after year carried them in its body: the lines, the hammers, the costumes kept in a guild's chest. Scripture wasn't only read to them. It was something they did.

Pick one Bible story you know well, Noah and the ark, the lost sheep, the Good Samaritan, and cast it in your head: who plays the boat-builder, who gets to be the stubborn one, and what would you use for props, a broom, a blanket, a cardboard box? If there's a child in your life, picture acting it out together; if not, walk through the scene yourself, just to see it from the inside. If you pray, you can give thanks for the story.
Mystery plays. Cycles of Bible plays acted by townspeople and their guilds, on wagons, in English, from creation to the last judgment.
Your line: the bible on wagons. A story you act out is a story you carry. Until tomorrow.

842.title: Pilgrims' roads
842.hook: Canterbury, Santiago, Rome: people walked a long way to reach a holy place
842.howItsDone: Christians, and others too, still walk the Camino to Santiago de Compostela, carrying a scallop shell and collecting stamps in a pilgrim passport, and pilgrims still travel to Rome, Canterbury, the Holy Land and other shrines.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mystery plays: the Bible acted on wagons by townspeople, with shipwrights building the ark. Your line was the bible on wagons.

Why would anyone leave home on foot to reach a grave? Part of the answer hangs from a walking stick: a scallop shell, tied on with a bit of cord. That's how you'd know someone was on the road to Santiago. Blisters, a small bag, a hat against the sun. They left home long ago, and won't sleep in their own bed for a long time yet. In Chaucer's tales, a company on horseback trades stories on the way to Canterbury. On another road, travelers climb toward Rome. Different roads, one question underneath.

Each road ended at a grave or a shrine. Rome, where tradition says Peter and Paul are buried. Santiago de Compostela, in Spain, where tradition places the tomb of James the apostle, and where the scallop shell became the pilgrim's badge. Canterbury, in England, where Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in his own cathedral and then honored as a saint. People went to ask for healing, to give thanks, to do penance for a wrong, to keep a promise. Some, honestly, for the adventure: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales is full of pilgrims who talk more than they pray. But the road itself mattered. Leaving home meant leaving your comfort, your title, your routine. On the road, a merchant and a farmer could sleep in the same hostel and eat the same soup, and monasteries and towns along the way took pilgrims in. Hebrews says the faithful of old confessed, in the King James Bible, "that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." A Psalm that longs for God's house blesses the one "in whose heart are the ways of them." And tradition says pilgrims sang another Psalm as they climbed toward Jerusalem: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." Christians haven't all agreed about pilgrimage. Some reformers later criticized it, saying God is just as near at home. Catholic and Orthodox Christians still go, and so do others, on foot. And some walkers say the same surprising thing: the road became the prayer.
screen: `A GRAVE OR A SHRINE AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Think of a place within walking distance that means something to you: a church, a park, a grave, a tree, a friend's front door. Picture setting out without your phone in your hand, carrying one intention, thanks, a worry or a person. If you pray, pray along the way in your mind; if you don't, let each pictured step be the attention.
Pilgrims' roads. The roads to holy places like Rome, Santiago and Canterbury, walked for healing, thanks or penance, where the journey itself becomes part of the prayer.
Your line: the road is the prayer. Every road began at someone's front door. Day eight hundred forty-two, complete.

843.title: Beads of prayer
843.hook: counting prayers on beads grew in the middle ages; the Orthodox use knotted prayer ropes
843.howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary on a string of beads, alone or together, and Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted prayer rope; some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pilgrims' roads to Rome, Santiago and Canterbury, where the walking itself became prayer. Your line was the road is the prayer.

A grandmother's hands rest in her lap, a loop of beads running through her fingers. Her lips move. Every few seconds, her thumb slides one bead along. In another house, in another church, a monk holds a loop of black wool tied in thick knots, and his thumb moves the same way. Bead, word. Knot, word. Neither of them is looking at their hands. The hands keep count so the heart doesn't have to.
screen: `A LOOP OF BEADS IN HER FINGERS.`

segments.voice: Counting prayers is an old Christian habit. Tradition remembers desert monks who counted their prayers with pebbles, moving one stone from one pile to another. Later, in the West, people threaded beads on a string to count the Lord's Prayer, the Our Father, again and again. In the middle ages these strings grew into the rosary, where Catholics pray the Hail Mary in sets, each set beginning with the Our Father, while they think about scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary. In the East, Orthodox monks use a prayer rope, a loop of knotted wool, and with each knot they say the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. They tell a story about it. A holy monk tied knots in a cord to count his prayers, and the devil kept untying them, so the monk learned to tie each knot as a little web of crosses, and the devil couldn't undo them. Whatever its origin, the story says something true about these ropes: each knot is made to hold. Why repeat a prayer at all? Paul tells one church, in the King James Bible, "Pray without ceasing." Repetition is one way people have tried to obey that line. But Jesus also says, in Matthew, "use not vain repetitions." For that reason some Protestants are cautious about counted prayers, and pray in their own words. Catholic and Orthodox teachers answer that a prayer said from the heart isn't vain, however often it's said. Each side reads the same Gospel seriously.
screen: `BEADS FOR THE OUR FATHER, THEN THE ROSARY.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap and choose one short line: the Jesus Prayer, the first line of the Our Father, a line from a Psalm, or, if you don't pray, a single word like thanks, or the name of someone you love. Touch your thumb to one fingertip and say the line slowly, then the next fingertip, ten times across both hands. If you lose count, start again without fuss.
Jesus Prayer. The words Orthodox monks repeat on a knotted prayer rope, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, so the hands keep count and the heart can pray.
Your line: counting love. Your own ten fingers can make a simple prayer rope. Back tomorrow.

844.title: The poor people's Bible
844.hook: colored windows told Bible stories to people who couldn't read
844.howItsDone: Stained glass windows still tell Bible stories in churches of different traditions, and churches sometimes hold tours or talks that walk people through a window's story from bottom to top.

segments.voice: Yesterday, beads and knots: the rosary, and the Jesus Prayer said on a prayer rope. Your line was counting love.

Late afternoon, and a patch of blue and red light slides slowly across a stone floor. Follow it up to where it comes from, and there's a window high in the wall, made of small pieces of colored glass. Look closer, and the colors become people. A man in a boat. A woman at a well. A shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders. A whole story, told in light, pane by pane, from the bottom of the window to the top.

Stained glass gets its color as the glass is made. Then the details, faces, hands, the folds of a robe, are painted on with dark paint and fired so they hold, and lead strips join the pieces like the lines in a coloring book. In the great churches of the middle ages, windows like these told the Bible's stories, and the lives of the saints, to people who couldn't read. A pope, Gregory the Great, wrote to a bishop who had smashed the pictures in his church. Don't destroy them, Gregory told him: what writing gives to those who can read, a picture gives to those who can't. Some people later called windows like these the poor people's Bible. Some historians wonder how much anyone could make out of a window that high, but even from the floor, the light did its work. Windows often paired stories, one from the Old Testament beside one from the New, so that Jonah coming out of the fish sits near Jesus rising from the tomb. Often you read them from the bottom up. John writes, in the King James Bible, "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." A stained glass window is dark from the outside. You only see its story from inside, when the sun comes through. Christians haven't all loved these windows. In some times and places, reformers broke them, believing images drew worship away from God. Other Protestants kept them and made new ones, and churches of different traditions use them still.
screen: `COLOR IN THE GLASS, FACES PAINTED ON.`

segments.voice: If you can, find something colored and clear, a bottle, a glass of juice, a colored jar, even a phone screen set to a single color, and hold it up to a lamp or a window. Watch the color the light makes, and notice that the glass does nothing on its own; it waits for the light. If you pray, give thanks for the light; if you don't, simply watch it.
Stained glass. Colored glass, painted and leaded into windows that tell the Bible's stories in light, once called the poor people's Bible.
Your line: light tells stories. Pane by pane, the whole story comes into view. That's day eight hundred forty-four.

845.title: Monasteries as hospitals
845.hook: monks kept books, schools, herb gardens and infirmaries
845.howItsDone: Christian religious orders and churches still run hospitals, clinics and hospices around the world, and some monasteries still keep herb gardens and infirmaries for their own sick members.

segments.voice: Yesterday, stained glass, the poor people's Bible, a story told in light. Your line was light tells stories.

Sage. Rue. Fennel. Mint. Small square beds of herbs in neat rows behind a stone wall. A monk in a dark habit kneels between them, cutting leaves into a basket. He isn't cooking dinner. He carries the basket across the yard to a long room where sick men lie in beds, to make a warm drink for a feverish old brother and a poultice for a farmer's cut hand.

In the middle ages, a monastery might be the place where the sick were cared for. The reason goes back to a rule. Benedict's Rule for monks gives a whole chapter to the sick, and puts their care before everything else, because in serving them, the monks serve Christ. Behind that is Jesus's scene in Matthew where visiting the sick is visiting him, the same scene that kept some at the bedside in the plague years. And the letter of James asks, in the King James Bible: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him". So monasteries set aside an infirmary, a room for the sick, with a brother in charge of it, and kept a garden of healing herbs nearby. An old plan for an ideal monastery, kept at the abbey of Saint Gall, puts a physician's herb garden right beside the infirmary. They kept books too, a slower kind of care. In the scriptorium, monks and nuns copied scripture, prayers, and old books of medicine and learning, page by page. Some monasteries ran schools, where boys, and in convents girls, learned to read. None of this was the main point. For the monks, the point was prayer, the psalms sung through the hours of day and night. But prayer that takes Matthew seriously spills out into rooms with beds, gardens with herbs and shelves with books. You could call these communities keepers of the light: a lamp kept burning in the chapel, by a sick bed, and over a page.
screen: `BOOKS, SCHOOLS, AND A LAMP BY THE BED.`

segments.voice: Picture a small pot of herbs on a windowsill, basil, mint, rosemary, whatever you like, and imagine pinching off a leaf and smelling your fingers. Now think of someone who's sick or worn out, someone you could bring a cup of mint tea, a bowl of soup, or just your company. If you pray, pray for them; if you don't, hold them in mind, with the smell of the herb.

Your line: keepers of the light. Care can be as small as a cup of tea. Until next time.

846.title: Guests as Christ
846.hook: the Rule of Benedict: let all guests be received as Christ (Rule 53)
846.howItsDone: Benedictine monasteries and convents keep guest houses where visitors can stay, pray with the community and share meals, and the porter or guest master greets them in the spirit of Rule 53.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the infirmary: herbs by the sickroom, and books copied in the scriptorium. Your line was keepers of the light.

A knock at the monastery gate, after dark. Rain. On the other side of the door, a stranger: muddy boots, a wet cloak, nobody the porter has ever seen. Could be a pilgrim. Could be a thief. Could be a lord in disguise, or a beggar with nowhere else to go. The old porter gets up from his bench by the gate, and the words he's been taught come out first, before any question about who this is: thanks be to God.

The Rule of Benedict, the guidebook for monks from yesterday, has a chapter on guests, and it opens with a startling instruction: let every guest who comes be received as Christ. Why? Because, the Rule says, Christ himself will one day say the words of Matthew's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." So the stranger at the gate isn't an interruption. In the Rule's eyes, the stranger is Christ, arriving in disguise. And the chapter gets specific. The superior and the brothers go out to meet the guest. They pray together, then exchange the kiss of peace. The abbot pours water over the guest's hands, and he and the community wash the guest's feet. Visitors are fed. The Rule adds a line that's easy to miss: the poor and pilgrims are to be shown the most care, because in them Christ is received more especially. The rich, it notes dryly, get respect anyway, because people are wary of them. It's practical too. The abbot and the guests have their own kitchen, so people arriving at all hours don't disturb the brothers. Holiness with a spare kitchen. The first letter of Peter puts the same welcome in a few plain words: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." Without grudging, even at the door after dark. The idea underneath doesn't need a monastery. Every door, sooner or later, has a stranger on the other side.
screen: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who'll come to your door today, in person, on a screen, in your inbox: a coworker who always needs something, a delivery driver, a child who interrupts, someone you'd rather avoid. Choose one, and picture them arriving, and yourself standing up and going to meet them, glad they came. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just hold them in mind kindly.

847.title: Margery Kempe
847.hook: a loud, weeping English pilgrim who dictated her life to a scribe, and wouldn't stop crying in church
847.howItsDone: Christians today read The Book of Margery Kempe as a window into late medieval devotion, and some find in it permission for loud, emotional prayer; the Church of England remembers her in its calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hospes, guest and host, and the Rule that receives every guest as Christ. Your line was receive them as christ.

A sermon is under way in an English church, and a woman in white is sobbing. Not quietly: loudly enough that the preacher stops. Some of the congregation glare. Some mutter that she's faking, or sick, or showing off. One friar, her own book says, refuses to preach while she's in the building. She's a married woman from the town of Lynn, a mother, a former businesswoman whose brewery failed. She can't read or write. And she has decided to tell her whole life anyway, out loud, to a scribe who will write it down.
screen: `SHE TELLS HER LIFE TO A SCRIBE.`

segments.voice: The Book of Margery Kempe is her story in her own telling, though she never calls herself I. She calls herself this creature. This creature went to Jerusalem. This creature was rebuked. It isn't a polished book. It's restless, funny in places, and honest about how much she annoyed people. The tears are its center. On pilgrimage in Jerusalem, the Book says, standing where Jesus was crucified, she fell down and cried out as if her heart would burst, and the crying came back again and again for years: when she thought of the Passion, when she saw a baby boy, when she saw a man being beaten. Fellow pilgrims got so tired of her that they left her behind. Clergy questioned her. More than once she was accused of heresy, and more than once she talked her way out of it. So was it holiness, or something else? Her neighbors argued about that, and readers still do. The Book doesn't settle it. But it records a visit she made to Julian, the anchoress at Norwich. Margery poured out her fears, and Julian, the Book says, told her that the Holy Spirit never moves a soul against love, and that a soul's tears can be a sign of the Spirit at work. Then, the Book adds, the two women talked together for days. The Gospels show Jesus weeping too. The King James Bible gives it in two words: "Jesus wept." Margery's neighbors found her tears too much. She kept weeping, and kept going.
screen: `CRYING AT THE PLACE OF THE CROSS.`
`JULIAN SAYS: TEARS CAN BE A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Notice what's in you right now, without trimming it down: if it's sadness, let it be the size it is; if it's gladness, the same; if nothing much is there, that's fine too. Think of one thing you usually hold back, a laugh, a thank-you said with feeling, a song in the car. If you pray, bring whatever is there to God as it is, not tidied first.
Margery Kempe. An English wife, mother and pilgrim who wept loudly at prayer, told her life to a scribe, and called herself this creature.
Your line: tears are allowed. What moves you can come to prayer untidied. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: you're Margery, in church. the sermon touches you and the tears start coming, loud. people are turning around. what do you do?
options: slip out quietly before anyone notices.
try to swallow it, and fail.

fork.reveal: the Book says she tried to hold the crying back, and it came anyway. she kept going to church, and on pilgrimage, tears and all.

chat.says: Who was Margery Kempe, and why do people still read her book?
options: A married pilgrim from Lynn who wept loudly at prayer and told her honest life to a scribe.
A nun who wrote a calm, polished guide to prayer for the women in her convent.
An anchoress who never left her cell and wrote down her visions herself.
chat.meaning: Margery couldn't write, so she told her restless, honest life to a scribe. Her loud tears divided her neighbors, and readers still argue.

this creature.meaning: Margery's name for herself all through her Book

Julian.meaning: the anchoress of Norwich, who counseled Margery

anchoress.meaning: a woman who lived in a cell attached to a church, for prayer

heresy.meaning: teaching judged false by church authorities

Passion.meaning: the suffering and death of Jesus
